title: For RL execution, how do you check that simulated fills are believable?
author: Alphanet_dogwalker
selftext:
I work with AlphaNet, and currently doing some work on improving order execution. You can take a look at the research I have done (https://alphanet.global/dynamic-twap-implementation-shortfall.html)   
Our research compares RL with Almgren–Chriss and flags simulator quality as a limitation. The part I'd like to understand better is validating the fill model once the policy starts choosing its own order placements.

Take a small-order strategy using L2 depth and public trades, with passive orders and cancel/re-post decisions. Assume market impact is small for this question. With aggregated depth, you have to model queue position; you don't directly observe which cancellations happened ahead of your order.   
  
A model could reproduce the average fill rate of a simple execution schedule and still be optimistic in exactly the situations the RL policy learns to select. Testing on new dates wouldn't necessarily expose that if the same fill assumptions are used throughout.  
  
So for anyone who's taken a learned execution policy from replay to live: which check actually revealed that the simulated fills were too optimistic? Was the useful comparison fill probability conditional on the market state, what prices did immediately after fills, or something else?  
  
I'm trying to understand what evidence would make the fill model credible for the new policy's orders. A concrete failure case and the diagnostic that caught it would be more useful here than an overall backtest/live P&L comparison.

comments.author: Rare_Inflation3178
comments.body: I’d validate it at the state-action level, not on average fill rate. Bucket the policy’s orders by spread, depth imbalance, queue proxy, order age and cancel/repost behavior, then compare simulated vs live fill probability and post-fill markout within each bucket. The failure I’d worry about most is selection-conditioned optimism: the policy learns to place orders exactly where the simulator’s queue model is weakest. A shadow run helps—send the live policy’s intended orders without capital, record exchange events, and replay those same decisions through the simulator. If the conditional fill and markout distributions diverge even when aggregate fill rate matches, the fill model is not credible for that policy.
